title: Latency attribution anchors and token-economics observability notes
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a working note for eng-observability + serving-runtime to converge on a) canonical trace anchors for attributing latency across the request path and b) a pragmatic approach to token-level cost allocation exposed in dashboards. Audience: SREs, runtime engineers, observability instrumenters, and product owners building model-cost reports.

TL;DR (short):
- Introduce a small set of stable trace/span anchors that let us reliably stitch client->frontend->router->model-server->gpu spans for tokenized inference.
- Capture token economics (tokens-in, tokens-served, model-variant, quantization-profile, gpu-seconds) as first-class telemetry and expose both aggregated and time-series dashboards.
- Prioritize lightweight, robust attributes that survive sampling and cross-process handoffs.

Why this matters (context):
We keep seeing investigation friction when latency regresses: dashboards show higher p99 but it’s unclear whether the cost/latency came from queuing, batching, model-hotpath, KV cache misses, or downstream client work. Separately, customers ask clearly for per-route / per-model unit economics. If we can join traces and token accounting, we can answer: "did this SLA miss cost extra GPU time?" and "which routes are burning the most tokens per retained value?"

Key definitions (proposed):
- client_perceived_latency: time from client-first-byte to client-last-byte (best-effort from edge).
- request_server_latency: time from ingress-router-accept to final-response-sent (includes queue & model execution).
- queue_time_ms: time spent waiting in request queue (router/local scheduler).
- batch_wait_ms: time added for batching benefits (per-request contribution).
- model_compute_ms: time spent on the model inference path (kernel-run + KV cache misses handled).
- kv_cache_hit_rate: fraction of requests (or tokens) answered from prefix/KV cache.
- tokens_requested: tokens in prompt plus generated tokens requested by client.
- tokens_served: tokens actually produced and returned.
- billed_tokens: tokens counted toward billing (may differ if truncated/policy).
- gpu_seconds: measured GPU-active seconds attributed to this request or batch (instrumented at runtime).

Canonical trace anchors and attributes (minimal set):
- trace_id: root id propagated by client-edge; always present when available.
- session_id: multi-request session grouping (chat session id).
- route: product-facing route or API path (e.g., v1/chat.generate).
- model_variant: exact model identifier + quantization tag (e.g., rdlw-1.3b-4bit-ptq).
- batch_id: identifier for a runtime batch (ties together multiple requests).
- batch_size: integer.
- kv_cache_key_hash: short fingerprint for recent-context cache (helps debug misses).
- gpu_device: device id or pool tag (for cost roll-ups).
- tokens_requested/tokens_served/billed_tokens: numeric attributes on root or final span.
- gpu_seconds: float (measured per batch, divided evenly across requests by default).

Span naming suggestions and placement: (keeps traces searchable)
- ingress: span.name = "ingress.receive" attributes: route, trace_origin, client_id.
- router/scheduler: span.name = "router.schedule" attributes: queue_time_ms, batch_id, batch_size.
- model-server/dispatch: span.name = "model.dispatch" attributes: model_variant, quantization, kv_cache_key_hash.
- model-exec: span.name = "model.exec" attributes: model_compute_ms, gpu_seconds, gpu_device, kernel_profile_id.
- response-emit: span.name = "response.emit" attributes: tokens_served, billed_tokens, response_size_bytes.

Sampling strategy (practical):
- Default: probabilistic sampling (low rate) for complete traces to keep storage budgets.
- Always-sample* when any of: queue_time_ms > configurable threshold (e.g., 100ms), model_compute_ms > X ms, or tickets flagged by anomaly detection.
- Session-first sampling: sample the first N requests in a session (N=3) to help stitch session-level regressions.
- Cost-sensitive capture: when a single request's gpu_seconds > high-cost threshold, always capture.

Token-level cost allocation approach (pragmatic):
- Measure gpu_seconds at batch level. Record batch_id, batch_size, and gpu_seconds on the model.exec span.
- Naive allocation: gpu_seconds_per_request = gpu_seconds / batch_size. Store as attribute on response span. This is cheap and deterministic.
- Enhanced allocation (optional): weight by tokens_served or tokens_requested if workload shows strong token variance per request. Provide both simple and weighted burn metrics in dashboards.
- Map model_variant -> $/gpu-second via a pricing table (config in infra repo). Multiply to produce estimated $ cost per request and per-route aggregates.
- Persist aggregate time-series: cost_per_minute by route/model_variant and cumulative cost by customer (tenant tag) for billing primitives.

Dashboard panel recommendations (concrete):
- Latency waterfall (time-sliced): ingress -> queue -> dispatch -> exec -> emit (p50/p90/p99). Use stacked bar view and ability to toggle by route and model_variant.
- Cost burn heatmap: rows=model_variant, cols=hour-of-day, cell=estimated $/hour.
- Tail drivers table: top contributors to p99 latency (kv-cache misses, large batches, kernel stalls) with triage links.
- KV cache hit-rate trend: tenant + global, with correlation overlay of p99 latency.
- GPU utilization vs cost: GPU seconds per minute vs estimated $/minute.
- Per-route unit economics: tokens_served per request, avg GPU-seconds per request, estimated $/request, request volume.
- Session-replay link panel: earliest sampled trace id for problematic sessions.

SLI/SLO proposals (for experiments):
- SLO A (interactive): p95 request_server_latency < 200ms for hosted tier.
- SLO B (cost stability): per-route weekly % change in estimated $/request < 10% (alert on sharp regressions).
- SLO C (reliability): p99 model.exec success rate > 99.99% (catch internal OOMs).

Instrumentation checklist (actionable):
- [ ] Ensure router attaches trace_id, session_id, route, tenant_id on ingress spans.
- [ ] Model servers emit model_variant and batch_id before batch formation.
- [ ] Runtime records gpu_seconds on model.exec and attaches to response span.
- [ ] KV-cache layer exposes hit or miss as attribute on model.dispatch span.
- [ ] Batching layer emits batch_size and batch_wait_ms.
- [ ] Aggregation pipeline stores per-minute aggregates for cost dashboards (route+model_variant+tenant).

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How to account for recovered work (retries/fallbacks)? Proposed: mark retries with retry_count and attribute gpu_seconds to final successful path; keep a separate "retry_cost" metric.
- Accuracy vs complexity for cost allocation: evenly split gpu_seconds is simplest; weighted splits by tokens are more accurate but require consistent token counts pre/post truncation.
- Data retention: we need full attribute retention for sampled traces, but aggregations (cost rollups) should be retained longer than raw spans.

Next steps (owners):
- Connor: prototype batch-level gpu_seconds emission and naive per-request allocation (PR in infra). Target: 2-week spike.
- Miguel: dashboard mockups (Grafana + query templates) for the 6 panels above. Target: next sprint.
- Sophie: add span naming and attribute docs to instrumentation cookbook and publish confluence page.
- Aisha (me): consolidate feedback and drive SLI proposal with product for hosted/API tiers.

Action items (near-term):
- Quick spike to add gpu_seconds to model.exec spans and emit batch_size (Connor) — unblock cost dashboards.
- Run 7-day compare report: current cost/hour by model_variant vs last week (Miguel) — baseline for SLO metric.
- Instrument KV cache hit attribute consistently across languages (Sophie + runtime owners).

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a small "cost debug span" that logs model_profile_id + kernel hist when gpu_seconds are high — keep only for high-sample traces.
- A simple epsilon correction for shared warmup costs (model load on cold starts) may be necessary — emit cold_start boolean.

If you have objections to any of the anchors or attributes above, add comments below this doc or ping in #obs-instrumentation. We should aim to land the minimal set in 2 sprints and iterate on weighted allocation after we have stable aggregates.

Historical references / inspiration:
- internal/obs/kv-cache-batching-metric-catalog (useful ideas but different goals)
- prior ticket OBS-203: expensive-p99-analysis (contains example traces worth reviewing)

End of note.
